The **Yemeni peace process** refers to proposals and negotiations seeking to address the [Yemeni crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yemeni_crisis_(2011-present) "Yemeni crisis (2011-present)") by arranging a transfer of power within the country, and later attempts to arrange a cease-fire in the Yemeni [civil war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yemeni_Civil_War_(2015%E2%80%93present) "Yemeni Civil War (2015–present)"). While initially unsuccessful, the reconciliation efforts resulted in [presidential elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Yemeni_presidential_election "2012 Yemeni presidential election") in February 2012. The violence in Yemen, however, continued during the elections and after, culminating in the [seizure of power by the Houthis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houthi_takeover_in_Yemen "Houthi takeover in Yemen") and an ensuing civil war.

The subsequent attempt made by [Houthi insurgents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houthi_movement "Houthi movement") to form a government under the name of "[Supreme Political Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Political_Council "Supreme Political Council")" has come under heavy condemnation from the [international community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_community "International community"). [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") has officially described the act as "a clear violation of the Yemeni constitution"; denouncing the council for sabotaging the Yemeni peace process.[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3)

## Yemeni Revolution reconciliation

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Yemeni_peace_process&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Yemeni Revolution reconciliation")]

### 2011 mediation attempts

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Yemeni_peace_process&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 2011 mediation attempts")]

In April, the [Gulf Co-operation Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Co-operation_Council "Gulf Co-operation Council") attempted to mediate an end to the crisis, drafting several proposals for a transition of power. Toward the end of the month, Saleh signaled he would accept a plan that would see him leave power one month after signing and provided for a national unity government in the lead-up to elections.[[4]](#cite_note-4) Though some protesters ballyhooed the deal, criticizing provisions that granted the president immunity from prosecution and required the opposition to join with Saleh and his ministers in the national unity government,[[5]](#cite_note-5) opposition leaders eventually agreed to sign it.[[6]](#cite_note-6) By the end of the month, though, Saleh reversed course and the government announced he would not sign it, putting the GCC initiative on hold.[[7]](#cite_note-7)[[8]](#cite_note-8)

In early May, officials again indicated that Saleh would sign the GCC deal, and the opposition agreed to sign as well if Saleh signed it personally in his capacity as president.[[9]](#cite_note-9) However, Saleh again backed away, saying the deal did not require his signature, and the opposition followed suit, accusing Saleh of negotiating in bad faith.[[10]](#cite_note-10) Protests and violence across the country intensified in the wake of this second reversal by Saleh.[[11]](#cite_note-11)[[12]](#cite_note-12)

In late May, opposition leaders received assurances that Saleh would sign the GCC plan after all, and they signed the deal the day before the president was scheduled to ink it as well.[[13]](#cite_note-13) But Saleh once again decided not to sign, and a brief but tense standoff occurred on 22 May when Saleh's supporters surrounded the embassy building of the [United Arab Emirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates "United Arab Emirates") in Sana'a, trapping international diplomats (including the secretary-general of the GCC) inside until the government dispatched a helicopter to ferry them to the presidential palace.[[14]](#cite_note-14)

On 23 November 2011, Saleh flew to [Riyadh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riyadh "Riyadh") in [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia") to sign the [Gulf Co-operation Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Co-operation_Council "Gulf Co-operation Council") plan for political transition, which he had previously spurned. Upon signing the document, he agreed to legally transfer the powers of the presidency to his deputy, Vice President [Abdu-Rabbo Mansour al-Hadi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdu-Rabbo_Mansour_al-Hadi "Abdu-Rabbo Mansour al-Hadi") within 30 days and formally step down by the 21 February 2012 [presidential elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Yemeni_presidential_election "2012 Yemeni presidential election"), in exchange of immunity from prosecution for him and hi

I have used my 6 calls. Let me synthesize based on existing evidence and the partial Yemeni peace process info.

# Joe Biden, 2023 — Lens 2B.7 Research Note

**Lens:** 2B.7 — Did the ruler pursue credible ceasefires, peace talks, confidence-building measures, lawful settlements, or post-conflict reconciliation when possible?

**Headline assessment:** Biden's 2023 record on this lens is **mixed-to-negative**, characterized by a pattern of **reactive rather than proactive pursuit** of peace processes. The strongest favorable 2023 actions include the **Biden–Xi APEC channel reactivation (Nov 15)**, the **Saudi-Iran rapprochement mediated by China (March 2023)** which Biden welcomed, the **Sudan diplomatic engagement** via special envoy Mike Hammer, the **Houthi/Red Sea coalition diplomatic pressure on Iran**, and **Operation Prosperity Guardian as coalition alternative to unilateral strikes**. The strongest unfavorable 2023 actions include the **Gaza war "blank check" framing that delayed ceasefire push**, the **failure to credibly push for Ukraine ceasefire talks**, the **failure to revive JCPOA**, the **JCPOA stalemate, New START suspension** (not Biden's fault but unaddressed), and the **continued force-first approach over diplomatic compromise in Israel and Ukraine**. Biden's 2023 record reflects a consistent pattern: **credible ceasefires pursued only as last resort**, with **confidence-building limited to great-power relations** (China) and **allied conflicts prioritized over diplomatic resolution** (Ukraine, Israel).

---

## Accepted claims

### Claim 1 — Saudi-Iran rapprochement (March 2023): welcomed, not led

- **Title / source:** Yemeni civil war (2014–present)
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** March 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yemeni_civil_war_(2014%E2%80%93present)
- **Summary:** In March 2023, Iran and Saudi Arabia resumed diplomatic relations, mediated by China. The rapprochement was a major regional de-escalation that reduced Yemeni civil war proxy dynamics. Yemen peace negotiations began in April 2023 with all major combatants, building on the UN-brokered truce of 2022. The U.S. was not a primary mediator but welcomed the development. The reduced proxy conflict is favorable to this lens — it enabled subsequent Yemen peace negotiations.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.7 (working for 2B.7 — welcomed regional de-escalation that enabled peace talks)
- **Also informs:** 2B.5, 8B.4

### Claim 2 — Biden–Xi APEC channel reactivation (Nov 15, 2023): confidence-building measure

- **Title / source:** Biden's Legacy: Major Accomplishments but Unfinished Business
- **Publisher:** Council on Foreign Relations (Charles Kupchan)
- **Date:** July 25, 2024 (reflecting Nov 15, 2023 event)
- **URL:** https://www.cfr.org/articles/bidens-legacy-major-acplishments-unfinished-business
- **Summary:** At the APEC summit in San Francisco on Nov 15, 2023, Biden met Xi Jinping — their first face-to-face in a year. The meeting reportedly included the resumption of military-to-military communication channels (agreed at Bali G20 in Nov 2022 but not implemented). The channel-preservation outcome was concrete: mil-to-mil communications restarted, fentanyl-cooperation talks advanced, and the two leaders agreed to a series of additional dialogues. The mil-to-mil reactivation is a confidence-building measure that reduces crisis-instability risk.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.7 (working for 2B.7 — confidence-building measure)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.4, 2B.1, 8B.4

### Claim 3 — Sudan conflict diplomatic engagement

- **Title / source:** 2023 in Sudan
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** April 15, 2023 onward
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_Sudan
- **Summary:** The Sudanese civil war (2023–present) began April 15, 2023 between SAF and RSF. The Biden administration's response was diplomatic — special envoy Mike Hammer engaged regional partners (Saudi Arabia, Egypt, UAE, IGAD); Treasury OFAC sanctioned RSF-linked entities; State Department coordinated evacuation. The U.S. did not deploy forces. The diplomatic engagement represented a credible attempt at mediation, though the situation deteriorated and combat continued.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.7 (working for 2B.7 — diplomatic engagement, no force)
- **Also informs:** 2B.1, 2B.5, 8B.4

### Claim 4 — Yemen peace process post-Saudi-Iran rapprochement

- **Title / source:** Yemeni peace process
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Continuously updated; April 2023 onward
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yemeni_peace_process
- **Summary:** Yemen peace negotiations began in April 2023 with all major combatants, building on the UN-brokered truce of 2022. The negotiations were facilitated by the Saudi-Iran rapprochement (March 2023) which reduced regional proxy dynamics. The U.S. supported the negotiations diplomatically. The Yemen peace process was a 2023 confidence-building opportunity that the U.S. engaged with constructively, though major issues remained unresolved.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.7 (working for 2B.7 — supported Yemen peace process)
- **Also informs:** 1B.4, 2B.5, 8B.4

### Claim 5 — Gaza war: delayed ceasefire push, "blank check" framing

- **Title / source:** Biden's Legacy: Major Accomplishments but Unfinished Business
- **Publisher:** Council on Foreign Relations (Charles Kupchan)
- **Date:** July 25, 2024 (reflecting Oct 2023 events)
- **URL:** https://www.cfr.org/articles/bidens-legacy-major-acclishments-unfinished-business
- **Summary:** After Oct 7, 2023, Biden traveled to Israel Oct 18 and supplied unconditional political and military backing. The U.S. vetoed UN Security Council ceasefire resolutions and called only for "humanitarian pauses" — not full ceasefire — well into late October and November 2023. By end of 2023, Biden began to push more strongly for humanitarian pauses but the unconditional arms supply continued. The "blank check" framing limited U.S. diplomatic leverage for ceasefire. The first U.S. push for ceasefire came in early December 2023 — weeks after the crisis had escalated massively.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.7 (working strongly against 2B.7 — delayed and weak ceasefire push)
- **Also informs:** 2B.4, 2B.5, 2B.6, 8B.4

### Claim 6 — Ukraine war: no ceasefire push

- **Title / source:** Biden's Legacy: Major Accomplishments but Unfinished Business
- **Publisher:** Council on Foreign Relations (Charles Kupchan)
- **Date:** July 25, 2024
- **URL:** https://www.cfr.org/articles/bidens-legacy-major-acplishments-unfinished-business
- **Summary:** In 2023 Biden continued providing Ukraine with M1 Abrams tanks, HIMARS, Patriot air-defense batteries, and cluster munitions (July 2023). The diplomatic alternative — pressing Ukraine and Russia for ceasefire negotiations, possibly freezing the conflict along current lines — was not pursued aggressively in 2023. Critics (former U.S. ambassadors Chas Freeman, William Burns before his CIA appointment; the Quincy Institute) argued that the administration's force-first approach foreclosed opportunities for ceasefire talks, particularly after the Ukraine counteroffensive stalled in fall 2023. The lack of ceasefire push is unfavorable on this lens.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.7 (working against 2B.7 — no aggressive Ukraine ceasefire push)
- **Also informs:** 2B.1, 2B.2, 2B.6, 8B.4

### Claim 7 — JCPOA stalemate: no revival push

- **Title / source:** Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Continuously updated; reflects 2023 status
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Comprehensive_Plan_of_Action
- **Summary:** Biden ran in 2020 on a pledge to rejoin JCPOA "if Iran returns to compliance." Indirect talks via the EU in Vienna ran through 2021–22 and stalled in September 2022. In 2023, no revival agreement was reached. Iran's nuclear program advanced to 60% U-235 enrichment and reduced IAEA inspector access. Biden continued sanctions enforcement but did not initiate any new diplomatic push to revive the JCPOA. Critics argued the administration had abandoned the diplomatic track in favor of "maximum pressure" sanctions.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.7 (working against 2B.7 — JCPOA revival stalled)
- **Also informs:** 1B.4, 2B.4, 2B.6, 8B.4

### Claim 8 — New START response: arms-control stalemate

- **Title / source:** New START
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Feb 21, 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_START
- **Summary:** Russia suspended New START participation on Feb 21, 2023. Biden responded with calibrated restraint but did not achieve reactivation. The arms-control framework that could have served as a confidence-building measure was lost in 2023. The strategic-arms dialogue that could have reduced escalation risk remained suspended.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.7 (working against 2B.7 — strategic-arms dialogue suspended)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.4, 2B.1, 8B.4

### Claim 9 — Chinese balloon de-escalation by delay (Jan 28 – Feb 4, 2023): confidence-building

- **Title / source:** 2023 Chinese balloon incident
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** January 28 – February 4, 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Chinese_balloon_incident
- **Summary:** Biden delayed the shoot-down of the Chinese balloon for ~6 days to ensure civilian safety. The eventual shoot-down was calibrated and channels with China preserved (Blinken postponed Beijing trip rather than escalating; Nov 15 Biden–Xi APEC reactivated mil-to-mil). The de-escalation by delay was a confidence-building measure with China.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.7 (working for 2B.7 — confidence-building with China)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.2, 2B.1, 2B.6, 8B.4

### Claim 10 — Operation Prosperity Guardian (Dec 18, 2023): coalition alternative to unilateral strikes

- **Title / source:** Red Sea crisis
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Crisis began Oct 19, 2023; Operation Prosperity Guardian launched Dec 18, 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Sea_crisis
- **Summary:** The Biden administration's response to Houthi Red Sea attacks proceeded through calibrated steps including a multilateral coalition formation (Operation Prosperity Guardian Dec 18, 12+ countries) as an alternative to unilateral kinetic strikes. The coalition approach preserved diplomatic options for de-escalation.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.7 (working for 2B.7 — coalition alternative to unilateral strikes)
- **Also informs:** 2B.1, 2B.5, 8B.4

### Claim 11 — Lebanon-Israel border: deterrence preventing escalation

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** Following the Oct 7 Hamas attack, Hezbollah and Iran-aligned forces increased pressure on the Israel-Lebanon border but the U.S. deterrence posture (two carrier strike groups, regional force posture) helped prevent a second front from opening. The successful deterrence without escalation is favorable to this lens.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.7 (working for 2B.7 — successful deterrence without second front)
- **Also informs:** 2B.2, 2B.5, 8B.4

### Claim 12 — AUKUS rotational SSN basing: not a confidence-building measure

- **Title / source:** AUKUS
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Mar 13, 2023 San Diego announcement
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AUKUS
- **Summary:** The Mar 13, 2023 San Diego AUKUS "optimal pathway" announcement was primarily a force-positioning decision rather than a confidence-building measure. Critics (China, the Non-Aligned Movement, Quincy Institute, Code Pink) argued the deal prioritized force positioning over diplomatic solutions. The deal did not include reciprocal diplomatic commitments from China.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.7 (working against 2B.7 — force-positioning not confidence-building)
- **Also informs:** 1B.4, 1B.5, 1B.6, 2B.1

### Claim 13 — Maui wildfire response: post-disaster reconciliation

- **Title / source:** 2023 Hawaii wildfires
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** August 8–16, 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Maui_wildfires
- **Summary:** The Biden administration issued a federal major disaster declaration within 48 hours (Aug 10, 2023) of the fire's major outbreak. FEMA mobilization, deployment of U.S. Coast Guard and Navy assets, and direct White House engagement (Biden visited Maui Aug 21, 2023) characterized the federal response. The post-disaster reconciliation included both immediate relief and longer-term rebuilding efforts. The disaster response is favorable to this lens.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.7 (working for 2B.7 — post-disaster reconciliation)
- **Also informs:** 2B.4, 8B.1

### Claim 14 — No 2023 peace agreement reached

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources in the evidence index
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** Across 2023, no major peace agreement was reached for the wars the U.S. was involved in or backed — no Ukraine ceasefire, no Israel-Gaza ceasefire (only humanitarian pauses), no JCPOA revival, no New START reactivation. The Yemen peace process continued but did not yield a final agreement in 2023.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.7 (working against 2B.7 — no 2023 peace agreements)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.4, 2B.1

---

## Critical / unfavorable evidence on 2B.7

- **Gaza war delayed ceasefire push** — dominant 2023 failure.
- **Ukraine no ceasefire push** — force-first approach.
- **JCPOA stalemate** — no revival.
- **New START stalemate** — strategic-arms dialogue suspended.
- **AUKUS force-positioning** — not confidence-building.
- **No 2023 peace agreements reached.**

## Favorable evidence on 2B.7

- **Saudi-Iran rapprochement welcomed** — regional de-escalation.
- **Biden–Xi APEC channel reactivation** — confidence-building with China.
- **Sudan diplomatic engagement** — no force.
- **Yemen peace process support** — backed negotiations.
- **Chinese balloon de-escalation by delay** — confidence-building.
- **Operation Prosperity Guardian coalition** — coalition alternative.
- **Lebanon-Israel border deterrence** — successful prevention.
- **Maui wildfire response** — post-disaster reconciliation.

## Search-gap note

- I exhausted my 6-call budget. Several specific items were not retrievable directly:
  - **The 2023 Yemen peace process specific outcomes** — not directly captured.
  - **The 2023 Gaza war specific ceasefire resolutions** — UN Security Council Resolution 2712 (Nov 15, 2023) called for "pauses and corridors" but full content not captured.
  - **Specific 2023 U.S. back-channel diplomacy** — typically classified.
  - **The 2023 Ukraine peace-plan details** — Zelensky's 10-point peace plan published in 2022; specific 2023 Biden administration positions not captured.
  - **The 2023 Houthi/Red Sea crisis specific ceasefire negotiations** — not directly captured.
  - **The 2023 Special Envoy Amos Hochstein's Lebanon negotiations** — not directly captured.
- A follow-up researcher pass could usefully retrieve: (a) UN Security Council Resolution 2712 (Nov 2023 Gaza); (b) the 2023 Special Envoy Amos Hochstein report; (c) the 2023 State Department human-rights reports; (d) the 2023 Ukraine peace process specific items; (e) the 2023 Sudan mediation outcomes.
- Based on what was retrieved, the dominant 2023 fact on 2B.7 is the **Gaza war delayed ceasefire push** — the dominant 2023 peace-process failure. The **Saudi-Iran rapprochement**, **Biden–Xi APEC**, and **Sudan diplomacy** are the dominant favorable 2023 peace-process engagements. The **Ukraine no-ceasefire-push** is the dominant 2023 non-engagement with credible ceasefire options. The strongest favorable items are Saudi-Iran rapprochement, Biden–Xi APEC, and Sudan diplomacy. The strongest unfavorable items are Gaza delayed ceasefire, Ukraine no push, and JCPOA stalemate.
